plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two panels, (a) and (b), tracking ten fractional values through a bucket sort. Panel (a) is a vertical column of ten gray cells headed by the italic letter A, with row indices 1 through 10 running down its left side; from top to bottom the cells hold .78, .17, .39, .26, .72, .94, .21, .12, .23, and .68. Panel (b) is a second vertical column of ten gray cells headed B and indexed 0 through 9, each cell serving as the head of a linked list. The cells at indices 0, 4, 5, and 8 contain only a diagonal slash. The rest carry a horizontal arrow into a chain of two-field records, each record showing a value on the left and either a pointer arrow or a terminating slash on the right: index 1 leads to .12 then .17, index 2 to .21, .23, then .26, index 3 to .39 alone, index 6 to .68, index 7 to .72 then .78, and index 9 to .94. Each chain is in increasing order, and the leading digit of every value matches the index of the cell whose chain holds it, which is the correspondence the two columns invite the reader to check. The panels walk through distributing numbers drawn from the half-open interval from 0 to 1 into equal-width buckets, after which concatenating the sorted lists in index order gives the sorted output.

interactionPlan.concept: Bucket sort distributes n numbers drawn uniformly from [0,1) into n equal-width buckets via index = floor(n*x), keeps each bucket's linked list sorted, and concatenates the buckets in index order to obtain the sorted output.
elements: Panel (a): vertical column of 10 gray cells headed by italic 'A', row indices 1..10 on the left
Panel (b): vertical column of 10 gray cells headed by italic 'B', indices 0..9 on the left
B cells 0, 4, 5, 8 contain a single diagonal slash (empty bucket)
Each linked-list node drawn as a two-field record: value on left, pointer-arrow or terminating slash on right
Horizontal arrows from each nonempty B head cell into its first node, and between successive nodes
Highlight overlay for the currently processed A cell
Shaded horizontal band over B marking the active bucket interval [b/10, (b+1)/10)

interactions.label: Bucket sort distribution

api.does: returns the value stored in input cell A[i] (1-indexed)
returns the number of nodes currently in bucket B[b]
returns the value of the k-th node (0-indexed) in bucket B[b]
inserts a new node holding x at position k of bucket B[b] — the ONLY way to add a value
attach a text annotation to the current frame for your own commentary

interactions.frame: the whole input array A with the current cell highlighted, the whole bucket array B with the touched bucket's linked list redrawn, and the computed interval [b/10,(b+1)/10) shaded
interactions.success_check: Concatenating B[0..9] in index order yields A in ascending order, and every value x resides in bucket floor(10*x).
interactions.teaches: The distribution rule index = floor(10*x) and the in-bucket sorted insertion together guarantee that concatenating the buckets in order is already the fully sorted sequence — getting either the bucket index or the insertion position wrong is immediately visible in the replay.

interactions.label: Test value x in [0,1)
interactions.teaches: Sweeping x shows exactly which bucket floor(10*x) selects and the half-open interval [b/10,(b+1)/10) that owns it — values like .12 and .17 both fall in bucket 1, .94 stays in bucket 9, and x = 1.0 is excluded by the half-open convention.

demo_steps.title: Run the distribution
demo_steps.narration: Execute bucketSort: each A cell is read in order, mapped to bucket floor(10*x), and inserted in sorted position. Watch the linked lists in B grow one node at a time, each chain already in increasing order.

demo_steps.title: Trace one insertion
demo_steps.narration: Step the replay to the cell holding .17: floor(10*.17) = 1, so it joins bucket 1 after .12. The shaded band over B marks the interval [0.1, 0.2) that this bucket owns.

demo_steps.title: Probe the boundaries
demo_steps.narration: Drag the test slider toward 0 and toward 1. Near 0.1 the value still lands in bucket 1 (not 0), and at 0.999 it stays in bucket 9 — the half-open interval [b/10,(b+1)/10) is what keeps every value in exactly one bucket and excludes 1.0.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because index = floor(n*x) maps each value in [0,1) to exactly one equal-width bucket and each bucket is kept sorted, simply concatenating the buckets in index order produces the fully sorted array with no further comparison between buckets.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two side-by-side panels. Left panel (a): a single narrow gray column of 10 stacked cells under an italic 'A', indices 1-10 down the left, values .78,.17,.39,.26,.72,.94,.21,.12,.23,.68 top to bottom. Right panel (b): a gray column of 10 cells under italic 'B', indices 0-9; empty cells (0,4,5,8) show a diagonal slash; nonempty cells emit a rightward arrow into a horizontal chain of two-field node boxes (value | pointer-or-slash), with arrows between nodes. Chains: 1:[.12,.17], 2:[.21,.23,.26], 3:[.39], 6:[.68], 7:[.72,.78], 9:[.94]. Use a light highlight color for the active A cell and a translucent band across the matching B row to show the active interval during the slider/code replay. Captions '(a)' and '(b)' centered under each panel. Keep node boxes uniform size so the linked-list structure reads clearly.

authoredContext:
Bucket sort assumes that the input is drawn from a uniform distribution and has an average-case running time of O.n/. Like counting sort, bucket sort is fast because it assumes something about the input. Whereas counting sort assumes that the input consists of integers in a small range, bucket sort assumes that the input is generated by a random process that distributes elements uniformly and independently over the interval Œ0; 1/. (See Section C.2 for a definition of uniform distribution.) Bucket sort divides the interval Œ0; 1/ into n equal-sized subintervals, or buckets, and then distributes the n input numbers into the buckets. Since the inputs are uniformly and independently distributed over Œ0; 1/, we do not expect many numbers to fall into each bucket. To produce the output, we simply sort the numbers in each bucket and then go through the buckets in order, listing the elements in each. Figure 8.4 shows the operation of bucket sort on an input array of 10 numbers.
To see that this algorithm works, consider two elements AŒi and AŒj . Assume
without loss of generality that AŒi _x0014_ AŒj . Since bnAŒic _x0014_ bnAŒj c, either
element AŒi goes into the same bucket as AŒj  or it goes into a bucket with a lower
index. If AŒi and AŒj  go into the same bucket, then the for loop of lines 7–8 puts
them into the proper order. If AŒi and AŒj  go into different buckets, then line 9
puts them into the proper order. Therefore, bucket sort works correctly.
To analyze the running time, observe that all lines except line 8 take O.n/ time
in the worst case. We need to analyze the total time taken by the n calls to insertion

evaluation.notes: The bucket sort structure (array A, bucket array B, sorted linked lists with correct values and null terminators) faithfully reproduces the source figure, and the code-editor workbench with playback, slider, and demo steps provides excellent pedagogical interactivity; minor issues include compressed node sizing and a latent len()-transpilation bug that does not affect the sample code path.
action_items: Fix the len() replacement in cExpr(): the replacement string '// @FIGURE_CODE_BEGIN.length' should be '$1.length' so that user code using Python's len() transpiles correctly
Increase NODE_W and NODE_H slightly (e.g. NODE_W=90, NODE_H=40) and increase NODE_GAP to better match the source figure's proportions and improve readability of the two-field node structure
Consider suppressing the yellow highlight band in the default (step 0) view or making it more subtle so the initial state more closely matches the clean static source figure
